newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Fuel convoy belies "total embargo" on Burundi.
newsitem.headline: Fuel convoy belies "total embargo" on Burundi.

text.p: The sanctions-busting convoy of fuel trucks, their number plates carefully concealed by mud, snaked through northern Burundi.
A mixture of profiteering and ethnic sympathies is helping landlocked Burundi and its Tutsi military leadership to soften the "total embargo" decreed by regional leaders after July's military coup.

An accurate barometer is the black market price of petrol and diesel fuel, the most vital smuggled import for the economy and for the military fighting a hit-and-run insurgency by rebels of the majority Hutu tribe.
After rocketing to five times the official price after sanctions were imposed on July 31, the price of a litre (0.2 gallon) of petrol in the capital Bujumbura has settled at around three times.

Some comes in jerry-cans strapped to bicycles or balanced on heads by porters using bush tracks across Burundi's borders with Rwanda, Tanzania and Zaire. More is ferried on dug-out canoes gliding across Lake Tanganyika from Zaire, witnesses say.
But the four-truck, seven-tank fuel convoy observed by a Reuters correspondent last Wednesday at Matongo 64 km (40 miles) north of Bujumbura, was no freelance affair.
Two jeeploads of soldiers, bristling with weapons, guarded the front and rear as the convoy crawled down the main road south, a winding gauntlet of constant ambushes by the rebels.
"This is the first convoy we've seen in broad daylight," one aid worker said. "Up to now they moved at night to keep this trade quiet."
The drivers had forgotten to black out one number plate. The letters TZB on a yellow background showed the trucks were form Tanzania, ostensibly the hardliner in the coalition ranged against Burundi.

The often divided leaders of East and Central Africa agreed on sanctions to punish the army's July 25 coup and to coerce the new military ruler, Major Pierre Buyoya, into accepting unconditional talks with exiled Hutu armed groups.
The government says the sanctions are causing a humanitarian crisis for Burundians, Hutu and Tutsi alike, and that unless they are lifted more radical elements could seize power.

Julius Nyerere, the former Tanzanian president and international mediator on Burundi's long-running ethnic crisis, is approaching devil status among many Tutsis. They accuse Nyerere of organising the sanctions and even government officials invoke a "secret agenda", implying Nyerere and the Tanzanians want to hand Burundi to the Hutus.
Prime Minister Pascal Firmin Ndimira, a Hutu who backed the coup, said on Friday the embargo had already cost the economy $162 million.

A report prepared by the government, in time for Saturday's regional summit on Burundi, said annualised inflation had risen to 40 percent from 19 percent before the sanctions and gave a warning of foreign exchange losses of $78 million if they remained in force until the end of the year.
Exports of coffee and tea, Burundi's main source of foreign exchange, have been successfully blocked.
But the picture for imports is not as bleak as it is painted.

"The idea of a hermetic closure of borders is really foolish. A country is not a closed room," the governor of Ngozi province, Lieutenant-Colonel Ascension Twagiramungu, told Reuters in his office this week.
"Anything that is possible, that is do-able to limit the effects of the sanctions, we will do," he said.
His province borders Rwanda, whose powerful army leaders are also overwhelmingly Tutsis. They were reluctant parties to the sanctions, diplomats say.

Hardline Hutus tried to exterminate Rwanda's Tutsis in the 1994 genocide there and the victorious survivors will not watch idly if the same threat faces their brothers in Burundi, the diplomats believe.
"The Rwandans want to help us but the government there is still fragile and cannot risk openly refusing to apply sanctions," one Burundian official told Reuters.
